content.text:
1) Answer

Short answer: You cannot “prove” that Pedro Sánchez, as a blanket matter, “disregards human rights.” What you can show is a mixed record: credible evidence of serious human-rights shortcomings in areas under his government’s responsibility (especially migration control at the Ceuta/Melilla borders and state surveillance), alongside measures that align with human‑rights protection.

What credible evidence says he fell short
- Ceuta 2021 summary returns of unaccompanied minors: Spain’s Supreme Court held the August 2021 returns from Ceuta to Morocco were illegal because authorities skipped required individual procedures and thereby violated minors’ rights. This was under Sánchez’s government (Interior Ministry). Later, a provincial court convicted the then central government’s delegate in Ceuta and a Ceuta vice‑president for prevaricación over those returns. These rulings establish unlawful state action affecting fundamental rights, even if they do not personally implicate Sánchez. ([poderjudicial.es](https://www.poderjudicial.es/cgpj/es/Poder-Judicial/Tribunal-Supremo/Noticias-Judiciales/El-Tribunal-Supremo-confirma-que-la-devolucion-de-menores-desde-Ceuta-a-Marruecos-en-agosto-de-2021-fue-ilegal-al-no-seguir-el-procedimiento-previsto-en-la-Ley-de-Extranjeria?utm_source=openai))
- Melilla 24 June 2022 tragedy: Spain’s Ombudsman found 470 pushbacks that day occurred without the legal guarantees Spanish and international law require. The Council of Europe’s Human Rights Commissioner said asylum access at Melilla was not “genuine and effective” and urged an independent, full investigation. Amnesty and Human Rights Watch documented excessive force and the lack of justice and reparations for victims and families. Together, these show Spain’s border practices and follow‑up fell short of human‑rights standards on Sánchez’s watch, though Spain’s Prosecutor later closed the criminal probe into Spanish agents’ conduct (no crimes found). ([defensordelpueblo.es](https://www.defensordelpueblo.es/noticias/sucesos-melilla/?utm_source=openai))
- State surveillance of Catalan figures (“Catalangate”): Citizen Lab forensically confirmed widespread Pegasus infections/targeting of Catalan politicians, jurists and activists (2017–2020), and the Council of Europe’s rapporteur noted Spain admitted 18 court‑authorized surveillances while other cases remain unattributed. Even with some judicial warrants, these findings raise rule‑of‑law and proportionality concerns persisting into Sánchez’s tenure. ([citizenlab.ca](https://citizenlab.ca/2022/04/catalangate-extensive-mercenary-spyware-operation-against-catalans-using-pegasus-candiru/?utm_source=openai))

Relevant legal/policy context
- Spain’s Constitutional Court in 2020 upheld the legality of the “rechazo en frontera” (summary return) regime specific to Ceuta/Melilla only if applied with real safeguards, individualized assessment and respect for international obligations—standards that independent bodies say were not met in the 24 June 2022 events. ([hj.tribunalconstitucional.es](https://hj.tribunalconstitucional.es/es/Resolucion/Show/26498?utm_source=openai))

Counter‑evidence (steps aligned with human rights)
- On international humanitarian law and arms transfers, Sánchez’s government first halted and then legally codified a total arms embargo with Israel in 2025, cancelled pending contracts, and paired this with humanitarian and diplomatic measures—moves framed by the government as compliance with Spain’s human‑rights and IHL obligations. These actions weigh against any categorical claim that he “disregards human rights.” ([lamoncloa.gob.es](https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/lang/en/gobierno/councilministers/Paginas/2025/20250923-council-press-conference.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: There is robust, well‑sourced evidence that serious human‑rights violations or unlawful practices occurred under Sánchez’s government in migration control and that accountability has been partial and contested. But the record is not one‑sided; some state actions, including the 2025 arms‑embargo package, point the other way. A fair summary is that the government’s human‑rights performance is mixed—strong evidence of failures in specific areas, not proof of a general “disregard.”

2) Sources I considered trustworthy

- Defensor del Pueblo (Spanish Ombudsman)
  [1] Source: Defensor del Pueblo (Spain)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Independent constitutional institution mandated to protect rights; high institutional credibility.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Its 2022 note on Melilla documents 470 summary returns without required legal guarantees; directly relevant and primary. ([defensordelpueblo.es](https://www.defensordelpueblo.es/noticias/sucesos-melilla/?utm_source=openai))

- Tribunal Supremo / CGPJ (official court site)
  [1] Source: Poder Judicial (CGPJ) – Supreme Court press release
  [2] Reasoning 1: Primary judicial authority; official communications on rulings.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Publishes the Supreme Court’s 2024 holding that Ceuta 2021 minor returns were illegal and violated rights; dispositive for this issue. ([poderjudicial.es](https://www.poderjudicial.es/cgpj/es/Poder-Judicial/Tribunal-Supremo/Noticias-Judiciales/El-Tribunal-Supremo-confirma-que-la-devolucion-de-menores-desde-Ceuta-a-Marruecos-en-agosto-de-2021-fue-ilegal-al-no-seguir-el-procedimiento-previsto-en-la-Ley-de-Extranjeria?utm_source=openai))

- Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights
  [1] Source: Council of Europe – Commissioner for Human Rights
  [2] Reasoning 1: Regional human‑rights authority; non‑partisan and expert.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Issued formal letters/statements urging a full investigation of the Melilla deaths and noting lack of effective asylum access; highly probative. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/commissioner/news/2022/-/asset_publisher/aa3hyyf8wKBn/content/commissioner-calls-on-spanish-authorities-to-investigate-the-circumstances-of-the-deaths-and-violence-at-melilla-border?utm_source=openai))

- Amnesty International
  [1] Source: Amnesty International
  [2] Reasoning 1: Long‑standing, globally recognized NGO with transparent methods.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Its Melilla campaign page synthesizes evidence of abuses and lack of effective investigation; pertinent and consistent with other monitors. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/campaigns/2022/12/truth-justice-reparations-spain-and-morocco-must-provide-answers-to-victims-of-human-rights-violations-in-melilla/?utm_source=openai))

- Human Rights Watch
  [1] Source: Human Rights Watch
  [2] Reasoning 1: Established NGO with rigorous documentation standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Spanish/Moroccan forces’ excessive force and lack of justice in Melilla; complements Amnesty and official findings. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/es/news/2023/06/21/espana/marruecos-no-hay-justicia-por-las-muertes-en-la-frontera-de-melilla?utm_source=openai))

- Citizen Lab (University of Toronto)
  [1] Source: Citizen Lab
  [2] Reasoning 1: Academic lab specializing in forensic analysis of spyware; peer‑recognized methods, independently validated by Amnesty Security Lab.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Primary forensic evidence base for “Catalangate,” directly relevant to state surveillance concerns. ([citizenlab.ca](https://citizenlab.ca/2022/04/catalangate-extensive-mercenary-spyware-operation-against-catalans-using-pegasus-candiru/?utm_source=openai))

- Council of Europe – Parliamentary Assembly working document
  [1] Source: PACE working document
  [2] Reasoning 1: Official CoE parliamentary body; balanced institutional reporting.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Records Spain’s admission of 18 court‑authorized surveillances and summarizes the broader allegations; helpful corroboration. ([pace.coe.int](https://pace.coe.int/en/files/33018/html?utm_source=openai))

- El País (news reporting)
  [1] Source: El País
  [2] Reasoning 1: Major Spanish daily with established editorial standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Reported the Ceuta convictions and background; used for contextual corroboration alongside primary sources. ([elpais.com](https://elpais.com/espana/2025-09-11/condenadas-la-exdelegada-del-gobierno-y-la-vicepresidenta-de-ceuta-por-la-devolucion-menores-marroquies-en-2021.html?utm_source=openai))

- EFE / AP (news agencies) and La Moncloa (official)
  [1] Source: EFE; AP News; La Moncloa (Gov’t of Spain)
  [2] Reasoning 1: EFE/AP are reputable wire services; La Moncloa is the official channel for government decisions.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Provide authoritative documentation of the 2025 arms‑embargo measures and contract cancellations used as counter‑evidence. ([efe.com](https://efe.com/en/latest-news/2025-10-08/spanish-parliament-approves-arms-embargo-on-israel/?utm_source=openai))

- Deutsche Welle (DW)
  [1] Source: DW
  [2] Reasoning 1: Public international broadcaster with solid editorial standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Summarizes the Prosecutor’s 2022 decision to close the Melilla case—relevant for balance on criminal liability. ([dw.com](https://www.dw.com/es/fiscal%C3%ADa-espa%C3%B1ola-archiva-causa-por-la-muerte-de-al-menos-23-inmigrantes-en-la-frontera-de-melilla/a-64199345?utm_source=openai))

- Tribunal Constitucional (official database)
  [1] Source: Tribunal Constitucional (Spain)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Primary source for constitutional jurisprudence.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Publishes STC 172/2020 on “rechazo en frontera,” crucial legal context showing limits/conditions often cited by monitors as unmet in 2022. ([hj.tribunalconstitucional.es](https://hj.tribunalconstitucional.es/es/Resolucion/Show/26498?utm_source=openai))

3) Sources I considered not trustworthy for this assessment (and did not rely on for key claims)

- Middle East Monitor
  [1] Source: Middle East Monitor
  [2] Reasoning 1: Advocacy‑oriented outlet with variable editorial standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: While it echoed Spain’s 2025 embargo measures, I preferred official releases (La Moncloa) and wire services (EFE/AP) for verifiable detail. ([middleeastmonitor.com](https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20250926-spain-cancels-third-arms-deal-with-israel-amid-gaza-genocide/?utm_source=openai))

- Anadolu Agency (for Melilla commentary)
  [1] Source: Anadolu Agency
  [2] Reasoning 1: State‑run Turkish agency; can reflect government framing.
  [3] Reasoning 2: For CoE statements I used the Commissioner’s official site and Reuters/Euronews summaries instead of Anadolu to avoid potential bias. ([aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/europe/spain-shouldnt-contribute-to-human-rights-violations-committed-by-morocco-council-of-europe/2750985?utm_source=openai))
